# Rust implementation

These rules turn K §11 to §15 and S §5, §8, and §12 into things to check while the code is on your
screen. The architecture contract decides where code goes. This skill decides how it is written.

## The loop

1. Write or adjust the test for the behavior (see `rust-testing-strategy`).
2. Make it pass with the smallest change that fits the contract.
3. Run `just check-fast`. Fix anything your change broke.
4. Repeat. Before handing off, run `just check` on the final commit.

The compiler and Clippy are feedback, not obstacles. Never add a crate-level `#![deny(warnings)]`. Warnings
are denied on the command line (K §12.1). A lint exception is a narrowly scoped `#[allow(...)]` with a
comment that says why.

## Types and APIs (K §11)

- **Newtypes** for identifiers, validated strings, units, money, and bounded quantities. Keep fields
  private, give each a validating constructor that returns `Result`, and add an accessor.
- **Enums** for closed sets and state machines. Match exhaustively when every variant matters (K §12.3).
- **Signatures.** Replace `fn connect(true, false)` with named configuration types.
- **Ownership.** Borrow (`&str`, `&[T]`) for temporary access. Take ownership to store or transform. Clone
  deliberately where it is clearer than lifetime coupling (K §11.2).
- **Traits** follow real behavioral boundaries. Add an abstraction after a second implementation, a test
  seam, or an architectural boundary is understood, not before (K §11.3).
- **Public items** stay minimal. Use `#[must_use]` where silently discarding a value is a bug. Rustdoc
  states errors, panics, safety, blocking, and cancellation (K §11.4, §18.2).

## Errors (K §13)

- Libraries and core crates expose typed errors, using `thiserror` or hand-written types, that callers can
  act on. Keep the source where it helps diagnosis. Never leak a dependency's error type through a port
  (S §5.3).
- Binaries may use `anyhow` at the composition root. Translate errors into stable exit codes or protocol
  responses at the outer boundary (K §13.3).
- Add context at architectural boundaries: the operation, and a safe identifier. Log an error once, at the
  layer that handles it, never at every `?` (K §13.4).

## Panics and arithmetic (K §12.5)

- No `unwrap`, `expect`, unchecked indexing, or intentional panic on a path that untrusted or operational
  input can reach. `expect` is acceptable for a locally established invariant, with a message that states
  the invariant.
- Where overflow is possible and meaningful, use `checked_*`, `saturating_*`, or `wrapping_*`. Plain
  arithmetic panics in debug builds and wraps silently in release builds.
- Poisoned locks, closed channels, and `JoinError` follow an explicit recovery policy, never an `unwrap`.

## Untrusted input (K §22.2)

- Validate before allocating or doing expensive work. Enforce the bounds from the contract: size, depth,
  decompression, parse time, and collection length.
- Do not build shell commands from input. Use argument-based process APIs. Handle path traversal,
  symlinks, and permissions explicitly.
- Use established cryptography crates, compare secrets in constant time when the threat model requires
  it, and use a secure RNG for tokens and keys.

## Async and concurrency (K §14)

- Keep blocking work off executor threads. Use `spawn_blocking`, with a bounded pool, or a dedicated
  thread.
- Never hold a synchronous lock guard across `.await`. Keep critical sections small and document lock
  ordering.
- Bound channels and task creation, and specify what happens on overload. Keep a `JoinHandle` whenever the
  task's success matters, and supervise background tasks.
- Put a timeout on every I/O boundary, and respect the end-to-end deadline. Define the cancellation safety
  of operations that mutate state.
- Retry only transient errors, with bounded attempts, backoff, and jitter, and only for idempotent
  operations (K §13.5).

## Configuration and diagnostics (S §3.3, §12, §13)

- Read configuration only at the composition root, into validated typed settings. Fail fast at startup
  with an actionable message.
- Keep secrets in redacting wrapper types, so `Debug` cannot print them, and test that. Never log
  secrets, tokens, or personal data (K §22.4).
- Use `tracing` with structured fields. Metric labels stay low-cardinality, with no user IDs, raw URLs, or
  error text (K §24.2).

## `unsafe` and FFI (K §15)

Use `unsafe` only when safe Rust cannot meet a stated need. Keep the block minimal, behind the smallest safe
API. Give each block a `// SAFETY:` comment that explains why the requirements hold at that site. Add
tests at the boundary, and flag it for specialist review. If the contract does not mention `unsafe`, adding
it is an escalation trigger. Stop and return `needs-decision`.

## Comments, TODOs, dependencies

- Comments explain why, invariants, and surprising constraints. Every TODO or FIXME names a card and its
  removal condition (K §12.6). Delete commented-out code.
- Add only dependencies the contract names, declared through `[workspace.dependencies]` (S §19.1). Anything
  else is `needs-decision` (K §16).

## Self-review before handoff (K §19.1)

- [ ] The diff serves one outcome, with no unrelated refactors or formatting churn.
- [ ] No debug output, dead code, or stray files. Generated files are called out.
- [ ] Every in-scope acceptance criterion has a test that fails without the behavior.
- [ ] Failure paths are tested where they matter.
- [ ] Public items are documented. The changelog is updated when behavior is user-visible.
- [ ] No new `unsafe`, dependency, configuration key, or public API beyond the contract.
- [ ] `just check` passed on the commit you are about to hand over.
